texts.orig: Demoting i686 Windows targets to std-only
texts.text: Demoting i686 Windows targets to std-only

texts.label: text
texts.orig: With Rust 1.100.0, the following changes to 32-bit Windows targets will happen:
texts.text: With Rust 1.100.0, the following changes to 32-bit Windows targets will happen:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: `i686-pc-windows-msvc` Tier 1 *with* host tools target will be demoted to Tier 1 *without* host tools.
texts.text: `i686-pc-windows-msvc` Tier 1 *with* host tools target will be demoted to Tier 1 *without* host tools.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: `i686-pc-windows-gnu` Tier 2 *with* host tools target will be demoted to Tier 2 *without* host tools.
texts.text: `i686-pc-windows-gnu` Tier 2 *with* host tools target will be demoted to Tier 2 *without* host tools.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Builds of the standard library will continue to be distributed, but host tools such as the compiler will be no longer available. `i686-pc-windows-msvc` as a Tier 1 target still undergoes CI testing.
texts.text: Builds of the standard library will continue to be distributed, but host tools such as the compiler will be no longer available. `i686-pc-windows-msvc` as a Tier 1 target still undergoes CI testing.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To build 32-bit Windows binaries, cross-compiling from a still-supported host toolchain (such as a 64-bit Windows ones) will be required from now on.
texts.text: To build 32-bit Windows binaries, cross-compiling from a still-supported host toolchain (such as a 64-bit Windows ones) will be required from now on.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Background
texts.text: Background

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Desktop and Server 32-bit only x86 CPUs are no longer sold for over 15 years, and general 32-bit Windows support has ended in October 2025. This means that the development platforms these targets are meant for hardly exist these days, and even if they do exist they typically aren't capable enough for development.
texts.text: Desktop and Server 32-bit only x86 CPUs are no longer sold for over 15 years, and general 32-bit Windows support has ended in October 2025. This means that the development platforms these targets are meant for hardly exist these days, and even if they do exist they typically aren't capable enough for development.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Even on the modern x86_64 hardware, building i686 Windows toolchains has proven to be problematic. We have encountered compiler binaries crashing when built with the i686 MSVC target, and the GNU C++ toolchain failing with OOMs during LLVM build.
texts.text: Even on the modern x86_64 hardware, building i686 Windows toolchains has proven to be problematic. We have encountered compiler binaries crashing when built with the i686 MSVC target, and the GNU C++ toolchain failing with OOMs during LLVM build.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Considering all these things, cross-compiling these targets from a better supported one is what we have found to be the best solution forward. As part of that, we stopped producing host tools for these targets. For the time being, the prebuilt standard library is still available, and in case of `i686-pc-windows-msvc` still tested on CI.
texts.text: Considering all these things, cross-compiling these targets from a better supported one is what we have found to be the best solution forward. As part of that, we stopped producing host tools for these targets. For the time being, the prebuilt standard library is still available, and in case of `i686-pc-windows-msvc` still tested on CI.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: What Changes?
texts.text: What Changes?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: After Rust 1.100, it will no longer be possible to install toolchains on 32-bit Windows hosts. We recommend cross-compiling from a still-supported host (such as a 64-bit Windows toolchain) instead. Other 32-bit platforms are not impacted by this change.
texts.text: After Rust 1.100, it will no longer be possible to install toolchains on 32-bit Windows hosts. We recommend cross-compiling from a still-supported host (such as a 64-bit Windows toolchain) instead. Other 32-bit platforms are not impacted by this change.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For more details about these demotions, see [RFC 3999](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/51783df9a76c355de7ceebeae101cba47f8ca463/text/3999-std-only-i686-msvc.md) for `i686-pc-windows-msvc` demotion, and [MCP 1020](https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-team/issues/1020) for `i686-pc-windows-gnu` demotion.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Rust 1.99.0 stabilizes defining C-ABI variadic functions with "C" and "C-unwind" ABIs. Variadic functions defined this way use a variable argument list ( `...` ) and accept an arbitrary number of arguments. Rust could already call externally-defined variadic functions (e.g., `libc::printf` ). With Rust 1.99, these functions can now be written in Rust itself:

texts.orig: The type of `...` is [`VaList`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ffi/struct.VaList.html) , which is ABI-compatible with the C `va_list` type across targets. What types can be read from a `VaList` is guarded by the [`VaArgSafe`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ffi/trait.VaArgSafe.html) trait.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: `Recommend against round-trip unleaking after Box::leak`
texts.text: `Recommend against round-trip unleaking after Box::leak`

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While there are no changes to the language semantics in Rust 1.99, we have updated the documentation on [`Box::leak`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#method.leak) to recommend against patterns that later deallocate that memory. This was done because such code was found to have problematic interactions with current and future potential compiler optimizations, and is especially problematic with the upcoming stabilization of custom allocators. Instead, [`Box::into_non_null`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#method.into_non_null) or [`Box::into_raw`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#method.into_raw) should be preferred.

This was done because such code was found to have problematic interactions with current and future potential compiler optimizations, and is especially problematic with the upcoming stabilization of custom allocators. Instead, [`Box::into_non_null`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#method.into_non_null) or [`Box::into_raw`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#method.into_raw) should be preferred.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: At the end of August, we [announced](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/08/26/announcing-our-first-maintainers-in-residence/) our first Maintainers in Residence, Rust Project contributors who are funded for their upstream contributions and [maintenance work](https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/01/12/what-is-maintenance-anyway/) from the [Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund](https://github.com/sponsors/rustfoundation) (RFMF). Since then, the Rust Leadership Council has dedicated more funds from its Project Priorities budget to RFMF, and together with AWS also providing additional funds, this allowed us to open a new full-time Maintainer in Residence (MiR) position to support the Cargo team. We would like to thank the Rust Leadership Council, AWS, and also the Rust Foundation for providing us with this opportunity! If you would like to help us hire more maintainers to improve Rust, consider [donating](https://github.com/sponsors/rustfoundation) to RFMF.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Why Cargo?
texts.text: Why Cargo?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The new MiR full-time position is dedicated to helping with the maintenance of [Cargo](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo) , our build system and package manager. The Cargo project is deeply involved in many new Rust features, improvements, and [Project Goals](https://goals.rust-lang.org/2026/goals.html#cargo-team) . Combined with its cross-cutting nature, where it has to support many different use-cases and integrate with several other tools, it takes a lot of work just to keep up with its maintenance needs, let alone support so many feature requests and proposed changes.
texts.text: The new MiR full-time position is dedicated to helping with the maintenance of [Cargo](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo) , our build system and package manager. The Cargo project is deeply involved in many new Rust features, improvements, and [Project Goals](https://goals.rust-lang.org/2026/goals.html#cargo-team) . Combined with its cross-cutting nature, where it has to support many different use-cases and integrate with several other tools, it takes a lot of work just to keep up with its maintenance needs, let alone support so many feature requests and proposed changes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Because of that, the Cargo team has sometimes struggled with meeting its maintenance demands. You might remember that for several years, it actually held a [feature freeze](https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2022/03/31/cargo-team-changes/) , to reduce Cargo's internal tech debt, perform necessary refactorings, go through the issue and pull request backlog, and come up with scalable internal development and design processes, so that they could eventually go back to even thinking about adding new features.
texts.text: Because of that, the Cargo team has sometimes struggled with meeting its maintenance demands. You might remember that for several years, it actually held a [feature freeze](https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2022/03/31/cargo-team-changes/) , to reduce Cargo's internal tech debt, perform necessary refactorings, go through the issue and pull request backlog, and come up with scalable internal development and design processes, so that they could eventually go back to even thinking about adding new features.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Recently, some changes occurred within the team, which made it more difficult for them to meet their maintenance baseline. Some members of the team left, while others lost their dedicated funding for working on Cargo maintenance and had to scale down their involvement. The Funding team thus considered it very important to support this team, given that we had an opportunity to do so. And thus we decided to hire a full-time maintainer to work on Cargo for (at least) the next 12 months.

texts.orig: We are very happy to welcome Scott Schafer ( [@muscraft](https://github.com/Muscraft) ) into the Maintainer in Residence role! texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: GitHub Actions leaking secrets when Miri output is cached
texts.text: GitHub Actions leaking secrets when Miri output is cached

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Rust Security Response Team was notified that Miri stores all environment variables to `target/` , allowing secrets to persist in caches.
texts.text: The Rust Security Response Team was notified that Miri stores all environment variables to `target/` , allowing secrets to persist in caches.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While not necessary a vulnerability in and of itself, when paired with GitHub Actions caching behavior, it is possible for this to expose secrets to PRs.
texts.text: While not necessary a vulnerability in and of itself, when paired with GitHub Actions caching behavior, it is possible for this to expose secrets to PRs.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Overview
texts.text: Overview

texts.label: text
texts.orig: GitHub Actions makes it possible to cache directories between runs. Typical setups allow CI runs on `main` (and other branches) to *write* to cache, and PRs can only *read* from cache (preventing cache poisoning). Rust projects tend to speed up CI by caching binaries built by `cargo install` and sometimes the contents of `target/` .
texts.text: GitHub Actions makes it possible to cache directories between runs. Typical setups allow CI runs on `main` (and other branches) to *write* to cache, and PRs can only *read* from cache (preventing cache poisoning). Rust projects tend to speed up CI by caching binaries built by `cargo install` and sometimes the contents of `target/` .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: PR CI can be triggered by anyone who can open PRs on your repository. GitHub requires maintainer approval for the *first* PR, but future PRs will rerun CI on every push. Anyone who has previously landed a change can trigger a CI run extracting information from cached `target/` and then cover their tracks by pushing a second commit to the PR.
texts.text: PR CI can be triggered by anyone who can open PRs on your repository. GitHub requires maintainer approval for the *first* PR, but future PRs will rerun CI on every push. Anyone who has previously landed a change can trigger a CI run extracting information from cached `target/` and then cover their tracks by pushing a second commit to the PR.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: GitHub sometimes hides overwritten commits in its UI, making this kind of attack harder to detect. CI run logs and overwritten commits are also deleted after a few months.
texts.text: GitHub sometimes hides overwritten commits in its UI, making this kind of attack harder to detect. CI run logs and overwritten commits are also deleted after a few months.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When `cargo miri` is invoked, Miri needs to retain build-relevant environment variables between runs [[1]](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/09/21/github-actions-leaking-secrets-when-miri-output-is-cached/#fn-1) . The current code to do so achieves this by storing [all environment variables to target/](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri/blob/165a9c3c96f0f4e6232278e62cb64648215bbc37/cargo-miri/src/util.rs#L40-L42) . This, of course, persists when `target/` is cached.
texts.text: When `cargo miri` is invoked, Miri needs to retain build-relevant environment variables between runs [[1]](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/09/21/github-actions-leaking-secrets-when-miri-output-is-cached/#fn-1) . The current code to do so achieves this by storing [all environment variables to target/](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri/blob/165a9c3c96f0f4e6232278e62cb64648215bbc37/cargo-miri/src/util.rs#L40-L42) . This, of course, persists when `target/` is cached.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If your environment contained secrets, these can now be accessed by PRs via the cache.
texts.text: If your environment contained secrets, these can now be accessed by PRs via the cache.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Our fix
texts.text: Our fix

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Our [short term fix](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri/pull/5337) for this is to make Miri only preserve `CARGO_*` environment variables (excepting `CARGO_*_TOKEN` ) and `OUT_DIR` . In the longer term, Miri and cargo may figure out better ways to inform Miri of the relevant list of environment variables. Note that this patch may not be available on nightly yet.
texts.text: Our [short term fix](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri/pull/5337) for this is to make Miri only preserve `CARGO_*` environment variables (excepting `CARGO_*_TOKEN` ) and `OUT_DIR` . In the longer term, Miri and cargo may figure out better ways to inform Miri of the relevant list of environment variables. Note that this patch may not be available on nightly yet.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We also performed an ecosystem scan of GitHub repositories and identified 1 repository with this issue and 7 repositories that do not appear to be vulnerable but should be cautious anyway. We have reached out to those maintainers.

texts.orig: Am I affected?
texts.text: Am I affected?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It is likely that our scan was imperfect, so we recommend you check your own GitHub Actions setups if you run Miri.
texts.text: It is likely that our scan was imperfect, so we recommend you check your own GitHub Actions setups if you run Miri.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You are vulnerable if:
texts.text: You are vulnerable if:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You run `cargo miri` in CI
texts.text: You run `cargo miri` in CI

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: The step that runs `cargo miri` [has access to secrets](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets#using-secrets-in-a-workflow) as an environment variable:
texts.text: The step that runs `cargo miri` [has access to secrets](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets#using-secrets-in-a-workflow) as an environment variable:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: By being passed in to the step itself as an environment variable
texts.text: By being passed in to the step itself as an environment variable

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: By being set in `env` for the workflow
texts.text: By being set in `env` for the workflow

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: By being passed in to a previous step that persists it in the environment somehow
texts.text: By being passed in to a previous step that persists it in the environment somehow

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: The workflow being used caches the `target` directory, usually done via [`actions/cache`](https://github.com/actions/cache) or [`swatinem/rust-cache`](https://github.com/swatinem/rust-cache)
texts.text: The workflow being used caches the `target` directory, usually done via [`actions/cache`](https://github.com/actions/cache) or [`swatinem/rust-cache`](https://github.com/swatinem/rust-cache)

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: The cache is accessible to PRs (common and often the intended use case)
texts.text: The cache is accessible to PRs (common and often the intended use case)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Possible quick fixes include:
texts.text: Possible quick fixes include:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Disabling cache for that job.
texts.text: Disabling cache for that job.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Scoping secrets to steps in that job that do not call Miri.
texts.text: Scoping secrets to steps in that job that do not call Miri.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Temporarily disabling Miri.
texts.text: Temporarily disabling Miri.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Once done, [please clear the cache](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/manage-caches#deleting-cache-entries) . Consider rotating any secrets that might have leaked.

texts.orig: The Miri release in the upcoming nightly (2026-09-22) will no longer have this problem.
texts.text: The Miri release in the upcoming nightly (2026-09-22) will no longer have this problem.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: **Even if you do not run Miri,** ensure jobs that can write to public caches do not have access to secrets. Many tools do not have special handling for secrets, and assume the entire environment can be written to the filesystem.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Threat model
texts.text: Threat model

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We consider it bad practice to have a cache that can easily be tainted by secrets.
texts.text: We consider it bad practice to have a cache that can easily be tainted by secrets.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If caching `target/` , it is worth making sure that the inputs to processes that create `target/` (anything invoking `cargo` ) do not have secrets available. It is generally rare for standard `cargo` build/test subcommands to need any secrets or tokens [[2]](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/09/21/github-actions-leaking-secrets-when-miri-output-is-cached/#fn-2) , so this is mostly a matter of being careful about having secrets exposed as environment variables to the entire job.
texts.text: If caching `target/` , it is worth making sure that the inputs to processes that create `target/` (anything invoking `cargo` ) do not have secrets available. It is generally rare for standard `cargo` build/test subcommands to need any secrets or tokens [[2]](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/09/21/github-actions-leaking-secrets-when-miri-output-is-cached/#fn-2) , so this is mostly a matter of being careful about having secrets exposed as environment variables to the entire job.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cargo/Miri/Rust does not guarantee that environment variables will be safe from being copied into `target/` . While we are treating this as a security issue and patching it out of an abundance of caution, this is not something you should rely on in general. Beyond official Rust tooling, it is possible for build scripts to be doing things that lead to the environment being stored in compilation artifacts.
